claims.text: A brief intermediate-temperature dwell during cooling increases atomic mobility relative to uninterrupted rapid cooling.
Increased atomic mobility during the dwell promotes homogeneous intermixing of the constituent metals.
Homogeneous intermixing favors a single-phase solid solution over phase-separated or elementally segregated structures.
Noble-metal HEA nanoparticles made by rapid heating and cooling typically exhibit phase separation, elemental segregation, or irregular morphology.
Insufficient atomic diffusion is responsible for phase separation, elemental segregation, or irregular morphology in the initial state.
The proposed intervention is an intermediate-temperature dwell during cooling followed by a final quench.
The target processing regime uses rapid heating above 1100 K and cooling rates above 10^4 K/s.
An effective dwell is expected at approximately 900–1100 K for tens to hundreds of milliseconds.
Initially spatially separated nucleation centers can homogenize by atomic diffusion during the dwell.
Dwell-enabled homogenization suppresses localized elemental clustering and phase separation.
Keeping the dwell brief prevents excessive diffusion, unwanted phase transitions, and significant particle growth.
Adding the dwell will produce a more uniform elemental distribution than direct rapid cooling.
Adding the dwell will increase single-phase solid-solution character and reduce phase separation relative to the no-dwell control.
Adding the dwell will improve nanoparticle morphology relative to the no-dwell control.
The proposed effect applies to noble-metal HEA nanoparticles containing more than five elements under nonequilibrium rapid-heating and rapid-cooling conditions.
Excessively high dwell temperature or excessively long dwell duration may cause unwanted phase transitions or particle growth.
The optimal dwell temperature and duration depend on the specific elemental composition.

Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in elemental homogeneity and phase purity, or observation of increased phase separation or unwanted structural transitions, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention describes holding at an intermediate temperature during cooling, whereas the mechanism describes a temporary increase in temperature. A dwell ordinarily arrests or slows cooling rather than increasing temperature unless reheating is explicitly included.
